title: A New Material That Lets Water Help Capture Carbon Dioxide
summary:
Factory smokestacks puff out carbon dioxide mixed with lots of water vapor, and that soggy mix has long been a headache for carbon capture. Now researchers at Oregon State University have built a material that turns the problem around: instead of letting moisture interfere, it uses water to help keep capturing carbon dioxide.

The material is called BVR-X, and it belongs to a class of materials known as metal-organic frameworks, or MOFs. MOFs are crystalline materials built from metal ions joined by organic molecules called linkers, forming repeating structures like tiny cages. Their extremely small pores trap gas molecules on their surfaces in a process called adsorption, much like a sponge holds substances within its structure.

BVR-X has an unusual internal structure that keeps water and carbon dioxide largely separated inside its microscopic pores. By directing the two substances into different regions, it stops water molecules from taking the spaces needed to capture carbon dioxide. Water usually makes capturing carbon dioxide more difficult, said Kyriakos Stylianou, a professor of chemistry at Oregon State University, but the new material responds to water by changing in a way that lets it keep capturing carbon dioxide even under very humid conditions.

That matters because many materials that work well in dry laboratory tests lose much of their capture ability in the humid conditions of real smokestacks. Drying the gases first is possible, but it takes extra equipment and energy, and those costs can make the whole process too expensive for industrial use.

Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas released when fossil fuels are burned, and as it builds up it traps heat and contributes to global warming. In the United States, industry accounts for 30 percent of total greenhouse gas emissions, according to the Environmental Protection Agency.
why_it_matters: Industry produces a large share of greenhouse gas emissions, so a material that captures carbon in wet, real-world conditions could help slow global warming.
